technique: line breaks — where the breath falls, and what the break withholds for a beat
poem:
The field below is caught between its colors,
the maples gone to rust at just the tips,
the rest still holding green they haven't spent,
as if the slope can't settle what it is.
Frost hasn't come, but it leans close each night,
a thing you feel more than you ever see —
the way a debt you've chosen not to pay
sits quiet in a drawer and waits for you.
You stand. The window gives you back the hills,
half-turned, half-stubborn, neither one nor other,
and that's the shape of most honest work:
a ledger never squared, a list half-kept.
But something out there counts on hands, not hope —

There are seeds waiting to be tucked into soil and cuttings reaching for the water — small living things that only keep going because you show up for them.

So — up!

lesson: Today, we work on one thing, the line break. A line break is the spot where a line stops and your eye drops to the next line, so you take a short pause before the sentence finishes. Look at the first line. It stops on colors before telling you which colors. You wait one beat, then you get the maples gone to rest at just the tips. The break makes you hold still, then hands you the detail. Later, the line stops on work, then drops to a ledger never squared, a list half kept. The pause lets the plain words sit before the specifics arrive. This works because the pause slows you down. You notice the last word of each line more than the words in the middle. The break holds back the next piece for a second, so it arrives with weight. Try this, write a sentence, then cut it into two lines so one line ends on a word you want the listener to stick with. The second time through, pay attention to how each break makes you pause before the final short line.
